content: The functions of health systems are aimed at achieving three primary goals: improving health, ensuring responsiveness, and promoting fair financing. Strengthening health systems involves identifying and implementing policy and practice changes to better address challenges within a country’s health system. This process includes initiatives and strategies that enhance system functionality, leading to improved health outcomes through better access, coverage, quality, or efficiency. Humanitarian and fragile settings refer to environments affected by social, economic, and environmental shocks or disasters, such as conflicts, post-conflict situations, transnational crises, natural disasters, or prolonged socioeconomic and political instability. In these settings, health challenges are particularly severe among mobile populations, internally displaced communities, and those in refugee or temporary camps. Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) are conditions not primarily caused by acute infections. They often result in long-term health consequences and require ongoing treatment and care. Examples include cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and chronic respiratory conditions. A health program is a coordinated and comprehensive set of planned strategies, activities, and services designed to achieve specific objectives and targets. National health programs typically involve coordinators at various levels (national, subnational, and local) and dedicated funding to support their activities. These programs often focus on specific health services, such as HIV prevention, adolescent health, or school health services. Programming refers to the stage in a sector’s planning cycle where newly identified priorities are translated into operational plans. While programming and programs overlap, programming can occur independently of a specific program as part of broader strategic and operational planning cycles. Protective factors are elements that encourage and sustain positive behaviors, reduce the risk of negative health behaviors and outcomes, and support recovery from adverse health events. For adolescents, protective factors include meaningful relationships, appropriate structure and boundaries, opportunities for participation and contribution, and encouragement of self-expression. Some conditions can act as both risk factors and burdens of disease. School health is a multisectoral approach to designing and delivering coordinated and comprehensive strategies, activities, and services within the education system. It aims to protect and promote the physical, emotional, and social development, health, and well-being of students and the broader school community. This term is often used interchangeably with school health program. Years of healthy life lost due to disability (YLDs) represent the equivalent of one full year of healthy life lost due to disability or ill health. Years of life lost (YLLs) from mortality represent the loss of one year of life, calculated by multiplying the number of deaths by a global standard life expectancy at the age of death. The Global Accelerated Action for the Health of Adolescents (AA-HA.) guidance aims to assist governments in identifying national and subnational priorities and implementation strategies to address the health and well-being challenges, opportunities, and needs of adolescents. It serves as a reference for policymakers and program managers in planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating adolescent health programs. The first edition of the AA-HA. guidance, published in 2017, built on the momentum of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the United Nations Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health (2016–2030). The second edition integrates learnings from the first edition, provides updated data on health determinants and outcomes, and incorporates the concept of well-being into programming. It emphasizes a holistic understanding of adolescent well-being and its implications for program design. Adolescence is a critical phase of human development characterized by rapid physical, cognitive, social, emotional, and sexual changes. This period requires special attention in national development policies and programs. Investments in adolescent well-being yield a triple dividend of benefits: immediate health and economic gains, future life improvements, and intergenerational advantages. Coordinated investments in health and education are particularly impactful. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the importance of global health investments and the role of schools in providing critical services beyond education, such as nutrition, social protection, and mental health support. This presents an opportunity to reinvigorate global commitments to adolescent health and well-being. Globally, adolescents (ages 10–19) make up 16% of the population. Over the past two decades, adolescent mortality rates have declined, particularly among older adolescent girls, but progress has been uneven across regions and groups. Leading causes of death among adolescents include road injuries, diarrheal diseases, and tuberculosis, with mental health conditions, iron deficiency anemia, and skin diseases contributing significantly to non-fatal disease burdens. Effective adolescent health interventions should address all levels of the ecological framework, from individual to structural. These interventions must be tailored to adolescents' specific needs and circumstances, delivered with quality and universal coverage, and supported by multisectoral collaboration. Schools play a vital role in influencing adolescent behavior and well-being through large-scale, long-term initiatives. National governments must identify and address adolescent health priorities through explicit, transparent processes involving all relevant stakeholders. This includes needs assessments, landscape analyses, and priority setting based on public health importance, vulnerability, and feasibility of interventions. Over time, priorities should be reassessed to adapt to changing needs and trends. Monitoring, evaluation, and research are essential for improving adolescent health programs. Countries should focus on priority indicators, disaggregate data by age and sex, and engage adolescents in participatory research and evaluation. Sustainability requires shifting funding responsibilities toward domestic resources and leveraging external funding opportunities. The AA-HA. guidance provides a systematic approach to planning and implementing adolescent health programs, emphasizing meaningful youth engagement, multisectoral action, and evidence-based interventions. It serves as a valuable resource for countries aiming to enhance the health and well-being of their adolescent populations.
